title: Rassapeague
summary: A Stony Brook Harbor swamp, meadow, and bay placename interpreted as a muddy or miry water place.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: In 1678, English colonist Andrew Gibb specifically petitioned for small islands of "creeke thatch meadow" located within the muddy, miry waters of Rassapeague Bay near Stony Brook. The preservation of this Algonquian place name in early legal patents demonstrates how deeply dependent the first European settlers were on the precise geographic and ecological knowledge of Indigenous peoples to navigate and claim Long Island's landscape.
introduction_content: Rassapeague is recorded as a swamp, meadow, and bay near Stony Brook Harbor. The land-paper description places creek-thatch meadow islands in Rassapeague Bay northwest of Stony Brook.
history_content: The land-paper reference describes meadow islands in Rassapeague Bay near the harbor mouth. The dated land-paper reference is handled as a timeline entry with citation notes.
translation_content:
Rassapeague is interpreted as a muddy or miry water place or cove, from elements connected with muddy or miry and water place or cove.

Why Place Names Matter

“Far from simple labels, place names are power-laden expressions of a community's identity, values, and ongoing struggles for recognition.”

— Tennessee Geographic Alliance, What's in a Name? Exploring Place Names as Forms of Social and Geographic Storytelling (2025), workshop introduction
preservation_content: Rassapeague preserves an older name for the Stony Brook Harbor marsh and meadow landscape, including small islands of creek-thatch meadow.
